labels.text: Two routes to immobility, neither route to unconsciousness
Persistent end-plate activation produces phase I paralysis.
Receptor antagonism prevents acetylcholine from generating contraction.
Sedation, analgesia, ventilation, and monitoring remain separate requirements.
A brief drug can expose long and lethal vulnerabilities
Denervation, burns, immobility, myopathy, and injury can amplify potassium release.
The boxed warning limits routine pediatric convenience use.
Ventilate and maintain anesthesia until objective recovery is complete.
Choose onset and duration together with the exit strategy
Rapid intubation is followed by variable hepatobiliary and renal recovery.
Organ dysfunction and active metabolite can extend block.
Organ-independent degradation is useful, but pH, temperature, and monitoring still matter.
Storage engineering and bedside protection must work together
Restrict access and use unmistakable paralyzing-agent warnings.
Confirm mechanical support, analgesia, sedation, and indication before dosing.
Maintain eye, skin, thrombosis, positioning, temperature, and daily indication review.
Match reversal to depth, then confirm recovery and airway readiness
Use adductor-pollicis monitoring rather than strength tests or elapsed time.
Match sugammadex or neostigmine to the blocker and objective depth.
Do not extubate until quantitative recovery and airway readiness are established.
